transcript.text: You mentioned executing manual test cases for a banking client's loan module and logging 210 defects in your first year. Can you describe a challenging defect you found and how you handled it?

I'm a test analyst at an IT services firm in Chennai, with about two years of experience. I started with regression testing on a card-statement portal, and then moved to a banking client's loan module. In the first year I logged 210 defects. Later I wrote test plans for two releases, which is a step beyond running test cases. I now want an MBA because I understand how the software fails, but I don't understand how the bank decides what to build.

You mentioned logging 210 defects in your first year and later writing test plans. Could you walk me through how you prioritized which defects to report first when multiple issues were found during testing?
transcript.anchor_quote: In the first year I logged 210 defects

transcript.text: My role involves working with multiple stakeholders in a fast-paced environment to ensure quality deliverables. I take ownership and drive results, and I believe I add value to the team and the organisation.

You mentioned working with multiple stakeholders to ensure quality deliverables. Could you share an example of how you managed conflicting priorities or expectations among these stakeholders during your testing work?
transcript.anchor_quote: My role involves working with multiple stakeholders in a fast-paced environment to ensure quality deliverables

transcript.text: The test-planning work for the two releases was my biggest responsibility. I listed the risky loan flows first, such as interest calculation and part-payments, and tested those before the screens. Two of my defects there were marked critical by the developers.

You mentioned two of your defects were marked critical by the developers during test planning for the loan module. Could you explain what made those defects critical and how your reporting influenced the development team's response?
As the owner of the test plans, I also had four testers reporting to me and I did their appraisals. That is the part of the job I am proudest of.

Earlier, you mentioned owning test planning for two releases and identifying critical defects. Could you describe how you prioritized the testing tasks within these releases to ensure critical areas were adequately covered?
transcript.anchor_quote: The test-planning work for the two releases was my biggest responsibility. I listed the risky loan flows first, such as interest calculation and part-payments, and tested those before the screens

transcript.text: I can't tell you the client's name or the loan volumes. Our contract with them is confidential, so I can only describe my own testing tasks.

transcript.anchor_quote: Two of my defects there were marked critical by the developers

transcript.text: I don't know what percentage of our defects were fixed before release. The developers tracked that and I never saw the final report.

transcript.text: I don't agree that testing is a purely technical role. Writing test plans needs judgement about business risk. So I would not say I have no business exposure.

Just to share, I am also trying to learn to bake sourdough bread at home. My first loaf was very hard, but the second one was better.

feedback.summary: The candidate has solid hands-on experience in testing banking software, showing understanding of risk prioritization and taking ownership of test planning. They recognize the business aspect of their role and demonstrate motivation to transition into business analysis and product management. However, some answers were vague on concrete stakeholder management examples, defect handling specifics, and lacked reflection on outcome metrics, limiting evaluation of impact and learning. Confidentiality constraints limit detail but clarifying contribution and communication would help.
